transcript:
Header: Date/Time: 2026-04-02 16:00 UTC | Duration: 55m
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Nova Tech CTO), Ethan Liu (Nova Tech SRE Lead), Sofia Alvarez (Nova Tech ML Eng)

Summary: Quick scoping to align on latency/throughput SLOs for Nova Tech's POC. Focus on TTFT vs TPOT, target percentiles, and how we'll measure them in the benchmark.

[00:00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. Quick intros, then Marco will walk through the measurement plan.
[00:00:12] Priya Rao: Hi all, Priya here, CTO at Nova Tech. We're mainly focused on responsiveness for our chat support feature.
[00:00:18] Ethan Liu: Ethan, SRE. I'll be coordinating the load runs and infra.
[00:00:22] Sofia Alvarez: Sofia, ML Eng, I'll share the prompt sets and expected mixes.
[00:00:30] Marco Diaz: Good to meet you, Marco from Redwood, SE. We'll try to make this practical — define clear TTFT and TPOT targets and measurement boundaries.
[00:00:42] Lena Park: Goal for today is to leave with concrete SLOs and a plan for the benchmark.

---
[00:02:10] Marco Diaz: Ok quick definition — TTFT is time to first token, that is user-facing latency for first response. TPOT we use as time per output token or per-token latency, that matters for streaming and long responses. Some customers call it per-token latency or throughput impact.
[00:02:35] Sofia Alvarez: When you say TPOT, is that average per-token or p95-per-token?
[00:02:40] Marco Diaz: Good question. We measure TPOT both as median and tail (p95/p99) because a small percent of tokens being slow degrades streaming UX. For POC we recommend p95 TPOT targets and p99 TTFT targets.

[00:04:01] Ethan Liu: For Nova Tech, typical prompt lengths — short queries ~20 tokens, medium ~150 tokens, long ~600 tokens for long context replies. Our expected distribution is 40% short, 45% medium, 15% long. Concurrency target is 120 simultaneous user sessions during peak.
[00:04:26] Priya Rao: Yes that's accurate. Also our business requirement: first token should feel near real-time in chat. So TTFT p95 around 300-500ms would be ideal; p99 < 800ms.
[00:04:40] Marco Diaz: That's reasonable. On Redwood we often see TTFT p95 of ~200-600ms depending on model and hardware; p99 depends on contention. For TPOT, we typically aim for p95 <= 40-60ms per token on optimized racks for medium models.

[00:06:00] Marco Diaz: Let's map that to measurable SLOs for the POC:
- TTFT: p95 <= 500ms for short prompts, p95 <= 700ms for medium prompts, p95 <= 1.2s for long prompts (because long prompts often hit more compute). p99 TTFT to be <= 1.0s (short/medium) and <= 1.6s (long) as stretch.
- TPOT: p95 <= 50ms/token for streaming on medium-length outputs, p99 <= 120ms/token as fallback.
[00:06:38] Priya Rao: Can you clarify how batching influences TTFT vs TPOT?
[00:06:44] Marco Diaz: Sure. Batching increases throughput (TPOT improves overall tokens/sec) but it increases TTFT for the first token if we wait to fill a batch. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching and adaptive batching: we set a max batching window and a latency cap to prevent TTFT regression. For the POC we'll configure small batch sizes for short prompts and allow larger batches for long streaming workloads.

[00:08:10] Ethan Liu: For the benchmark, we want both steady-state throughput and peak spike runs. How long should each test run be to get stable p95/p99?
[00:08:18] Marco Diaz: We recommend 30-60 minute steady-state runs for p99 stability, plus shorter spike runs (5-10 minutes) to validate autoscaling. We'll capture TTFT/TPOT distributions across runs.
[00:08:30] Sofia Alvarez: Are you using wrk or a custom harness?
[00:08:34] Marco Diaz: We'll supply a wrk-based harness and a Redwood-specific agent that can stream tokens and measure per-token timestamps. We'll include a script and a shared spreadsheet to collect results.

[00:09:05] Lena Park: Quick note on measurement windows — we will report p95/p99 over the whole run, and also per-minute rolling p99 to find spikes. That helps debug noisy tails.

[00:10:20] Priya Rao: Security question — does benchmarking with Redwood require sharing any sensitive data? We prefer to obfuscate user PII in the prompt set.
[00:10:29] Marco Diaz: Absolutely. Use synthetic or redacted prompts. If needed we can run an on-prem/private run for the benchmark — but initially a hosted run with redacted prompts is fine.

[00:11:00] Ethan Liu: For capacity planning: with 120 concurrent sessions, what's the expected req/s? We saw earlier Nova Tech's median turn length is 150 tokens, say average reply 120 tokens.
[00:11:13] Marco Diaz: Rough math: if each session issues 0.02 requests/sec average, that's ~2.4 RPS; but human chat is bursty. For safety let's target a synthetic peak of 60 RPS and sustained 20 RPS. We'll validate in the POC.
[00:11:30] Sofia Alvarez: Can we include rate-limited experiments? We want to see graceful degradation and fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
[00:11:37] Marco Diaz: Yes, Redwood supports routing policies and can fallback to smaller quantized variants. As part of the benchmark we'll run an A/B: baseline model vs quantized/downgrade path to measure cost/latency tradeoffs.

[00:13:00] Lena Park: Let's document success criteria for the POC — what would Nova Tech consider a win?
[00:13:06] Priya Rao: 1) Meet TTFT p95 targets for short/medium prompts in our steady-state runs. 2) Acceptable TPOT p95 so streaming UX is smooth. 3) Demonstrated autoscaling and fallback that keeps error rate < 0.5% under peak. 4) Clear cost estimate per 1M tokens with recommended config.
[00:13:28] Marco Diaz: I'll add one: reproducible benchmark steps and dashboard so Nova Tech can re-run.

[00:14:10] Ethan Liu: On metrics collection — we want both client-side metrics (timestamps at client for TTFT) and server-side metrics (Redwood tracing for scheduling/batching delays).
[00:14:22] Marco Diaz: We'll instrument both. Client timestamps show end-to-end TTFT; Redwood will provide per-stage timings: scheduling queue time, batch waiting time, kernel execution, KV cache hit rate. Note that transcriptions sometimes show product names wrong — sorry, just filler — but the traces will be precise.

[00:15:45] Priya Rao: For p95 targets, is it OK to set slightly different targets per prompt size?
[00:15:51] Marco Diaz: Yes, that's the recommendation. Short prompts: TTFT p95 target 300-500ms. Medium: p95 500-700ms. Long: p95 up to 1.2s. We'll call these the POC SLO buckets.

[00:17:30] Sofia Alvarez: What about cold-start vs warm sessions? We see higher TTFT for cold kv-cache misses.
[00:17:36] Marco Diaz: Good point. We'll measure warm vs cold separately. POC SLO will be defined on warm path (steady-state), but we'll also report cold-start p95 metrics. If cold misses are unacceptable we can recommend pinned instances or pre-warm strategies.

[00:19:00] Lena Park: Timeline recap: Redwood sends benchmark plan by 4/5, Nova Tech shares prompts by 4/7, joint run ~4/12. Results and cost estimate within 3 business days after runs. Any objections?
[00:19:14] Priya Rao: Sounds good.

[00:20:05] Marco Diaz: A few measurement specifics to include in the plan:
- Sampling rate for traces: full trace for 1% of requests, aggregated histograms for p95/p99 across all.
- Measurement window: 30 minutes steady-state, 10x warm-up excluded from reporting.
- Percentiles: report p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, and token throughput (tokens/sec) for each run.
- Error budget: <0.5% 5xx errors for success.

[00:22:00] Ethan Liu: For hardware baselines, will Redwood provide the instance types and estimated costs?
[00:22:06] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll include model variant, GPU type, quantization profile, and an estimated cost per hour and per 1M tokens. We'll also show a cost/latency curve for different batch settings.

[00:24:10] Priya Rao: If we don't meet the SLOs on hosted infra, can we try a dedicated pool?
[00:24:17] Marco Diaz: Absolutely. That's part of the evaluation matrix — hosted (shared) vs dedicated vs private. We'll include a dedicated run if needed.

[00:26:05] Sofia Alvarez: On measurement noise — what's tolerable variance for p99 across runs?
[00:26:12] Marco Diaz: We expect p99 variance to be higher; aim for less than 20% variance across repeated steady-state runs. If it's higher, we dig into queuing/batching spikes.

[00:28:30] Lena Park: Ok let's craft the POC success criteria final phrasing:
- TTFT: p95 <= 500ms (short), <=700ms (medium), <=1.2s (long) in steady-state runs.
- TPOT: p95 <= 50ms/token for medium outputs; p99 <= 120ms/token.
- Throughput: sustained 20 RPS baseline, 60 RPS peak with autoscale within expected window.
- Errors: <0.5% error rate.
- Measurement: 30-minute steady-state runs, p95/p99 reported, client+server traces attached.

[00:30:00] Priya Rao: That matches our internal bar. A question on TTL for KV cache — if the model uses KV cache across turns do you account that?
[00:30:09] Marco Diaz: Yes KV cache hit rate is a dimension in the benchmark. We will run scenarios with cold cache and warm cache handshake. KV cache TTLs are configurable. For chat continuity you'll likely get high hit rates after the session starts.

[00:31:45] Ethan Liu: We'll need a reproducible script to generate token-level timestamps.
[00:31:50] Marco Diaz: We'll provide the harness that logs: request sent, first token received timestamp, every token timestamp. That gives per-token TPOT derivation. We'll aggregate and publish histograms.

[00:33:20] Sofia Alvarez: Any other pitfalls to watch for? We've seen spikes due to autoscaler cold launches in other systems.
[00:33:27] Marco Diaz: Right, we'll include an autoscale warm-up test to validate the scaling delay. Redwood's Dedicated pools minimize cold start; for hosted you can see spikes. We'll simulate cold-launch spike to document it.

[00:35:10] Lena Park: Quick note — we'll also include recommended runtime config: batch window ms, max batch size, quantization profile. That way we can map cost to latency.

[00:36:45] Priya Rao: For the cost estimate, can you provide per-1M token cost for both baseline and quantized paths?
[00:36:52] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll include that. Expect quantized variants to be 30-60% cheaper depending on model and quality tradeoff. We'll show quality delta vs cost.

[00:38:20] Ethan Liu: Anything about SLO enforcement? This is a POC, but we want to know how Redwood surfaces SLO breaches.
[00:38:27] Marco Diaz: Redwood Console will show per-route p50/p95/p99, alerts can be configured for breaches. For the POC we'll set alert thresholds and a runbook to triage.

[00:40:00] Sofia Alvarez: Can you include an example dashboard layout in the materials?
[00:40:05] Marco Diaz: Yes, included in the benchmark pack.

[00:42:10] Lena Park: Anything else from Nova Tech?
[00:42:15] Priya Rao: No, just want to ensure we get clear pass/fail metrics and costs after the run.
[00:42:20] Ethan Liu: Also include the raw logs and histograms so we can do our own analysis.
[00:42:25] Marco Diaz: We'll share both aggregated reports and raw traces for the joint team.

[00:44:00] Lena Park: Great. Recap of next steps: Redwood sends plan by 4/5, Nova Tech shares prompts by 4/7, joint run 4/12, results + cost within 3 business days.
[00:44:15] Priya Rao: Confirmed.

[00:44:20] Sofia Alvarez: Confirmed.

[00:45:00] Lena Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
[00:45:05] Marco Diaz: Thanks all.

[00:54:55] (call ended)
